1.pericope_label: When Ephraim spake trembling, he exalted himself in Israel; but when he offended in Baal, he died
debates: Whether the trembling is the humility of Ephraim or the terror he inspired
What the exaltation refers to
When the death of Ephraim took place
outliers: Calvin sets aside every reading that makes the trembling the dread of the people at a new worship, holding that the verse states the twofold state of the kingdom and that its fall was its own fault
Ellicott renders the clause as uttering terror and refers the whole to the revolt of the ten tribes, where Clarke and Wesley read a contrite spirit exalted
themes: A tribe heard with reverence while it spoke humbly
A younger son preferred to the first-begotten
A happy ignorance of what one ought not to meddle with
A people who take something for God and expect it to save them

2.pericope_label: They say of them, Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves
debates: Whether the phrase means those who sacrifice men or sacrificers from among men
What the kissing of the calves was
What the four similitudes are meant to show
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both reject the rendering that would make human sacrifice part of the calf-worship, arguing that such offerings belonged to another cult whose worshippers did not kiss calves
Clarke reads the clause as a practical test by which a doubtful convert could be identified, rather than as a description of what the idolaters said
themes: Silver given for commerce and turned into a god
An idol too high to reach, kissed at second hand from the palm
A morning cloud gone as soon as the sun is up
Smoke from a lattice, dispersing as it leaves the roof

4.pericope_label: According to their pasture, so were they filled; they were filled, and their heart was exalted; therefore have they forgotten me
debates: Whether a long addition in the Greek belongs to the text
What it means that God knew them in the wilderness
Why plenty produced forgetfulness
outliers: Clarke suggests the Greek addition may once have stood in the Hebrew text, where Ellicott reports that Jerome could find it in no Hebrew copy and judged it spurious
Calvin makes the verb know a matter of two knowledges, ours and God own, and argues from a saying of Paul that being known first is what makes ingratitude shameful
themes: A people taught from infancy and so left without excuse
A country of bondage that was to them like the grave
A friend at need who could victual an army where nothing grew
A flock brought from short commons into fat pasture

7.pericope_label: Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I observe them
debates: Whether the verbs are future or already begun
What the caul of the heart is
Why God is described under the figure of beasts at all
outliers: Ellicott reports a variant reading behind the Greek, Latin and Syriac versions which turns the clause into a panther on the way to Assyria
Calvin rejects the reading that makes the enclosure of the heart the obstinacy of the people, calling it over-refined, though he allows the prophet may glance at it
themes: A lion the slower for its age and the crueller for its grip
A spotted beast lying in thick cover beside a road
A bear robbed of the whelps it had licked into shape
A God who puts on another character because men will not let him keep his own

9.pericope_label: O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself; but in me is thine help
debates: What it is that has destroyed them
Whether the second clause offers help or charges rebellion
How the figures of the beasts square with self-destruction
outliers: Ellicott renders the closing words as a charge that their help was against God, supplying a verb of rebellion, where every other voice reads an offer of help
Calvin declines both the calf and the change of person and takes the verb indefinitely, so that the verse asks who has destroyed them rather than naming the destroyer
themes: A God cleared of an imputation by the mouth of the people he punishes
A consuming fire in whom they might have had help
A plank thrown out after shipwreck
Offers of rescue opposed by the men they were meant to save

10.pericope_label: I gave thee a king in mine anger, and took him away in my wrath
debates: Whether the opening clause is a promise or a taunt
Which king was given in anger
What the binding up of the iniquity means
outliers: Calvin refers the king given in anger to the founder of the northern kingdom and makes the whole monarchy a cursed beginning, where Gill and Clarke name the first king of the united nation and Ellicott the entire succession
Ellicott corrects the tenses to the present, so that the giving and taking away describe a continuing practice rather than a single act
themes: A king asked for and granted in anger
A God unchanged, whose favour is closed off from the other side
Sins bound in a bundle and kept for production in open court
A sealed writing that lasts precisely because it is not published

13.pericope_label: I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death
debates: Whether the ransom from the grave is a promise or a question expecting no
What the delay in the birth stands for
How the last clause about repentance is to be taken
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch name Calvin among the commentators who put force upon the words by making the verse conditional or interrogative, and insist it is a promise and not a threat
Ellicott sets out both readings and objects to the promise on the ground that the prophet rushes in the same breath to the most sweeping condemnation
themes: A child that sticks in the birth and dies of the delay
A captivity read as a grave, and a people as dry bones
A Prince of life who goes under the power he means to destroy
Death and the grave summoned to do their worst as they are about to perish

15.pericope_label: An east wind shall come, the wind of the Lord shall come up from the wilderness, and his spring shall become dry
debates: Whose fruitfulness the opening clause describes
Whether the particle that opens the verse is causal, temporal or conditional
Where the last verse of the chapter belongs
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch make the verse a proof that the promise of redemption stands firm, arguing from the particle that no conditional or hypothetical rendering is grammatically possible
Gill sets aside a reading which takes the fruitfulness of the Redeemer who increases his brethren, and refers it to the tribe instead
themes: A name that means fruitfulness, played upon in the verb beside it
A younger brother preferred, and the honour turned into pride
A hot wind off the desert, blasting a spring dry
A chapter division that cuts a sentence from its explanation
